column1: # suites.tsv - what each suite is, and which lanes run it.
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Alexandre Gomes Gaigalas <alganet@gmail.com>
# SPDX-License-Identifier: ISC
# suite <TAB> lanes <TAB> setup <TAB> command
# This had sixty-two rows for eighteen suites, because a row was one suite on
# one lane and five lanes ran nearly the same list. Twenty-nine of those rows
# were duplicates of another: `verify-std.sh doc` appeared five times, and the
# file could not say that the five were one thing.
# `lanes` is a space-separated list, or `*` for every lane, which is exactly how
# cases.tsv's `applies-to` already works -- and, as there, no row says `*` any
# more. Four did, and they meant the five desktop lanes: the day
# windows-launch and macos-netinstall got a row each for netinstall, `*` began
# claiming the standards probes for two lanes that have never run them, and
# selftest's dormant-row check said so. A list is what a row knows; "every
# lane" is a fact about the other file. A suite that genuinely differs takes a
# second row with a disjoint lane list -- walk runs the release build on gjs and
# the testing build on kde, and that is a fact worth two rows. Disjoint and not
# ordered: which row applies to a lane is never a question of precedence, and
# selftest asserts no lane is claimed twice for one suite.
# `setup` is space-separated directives from the closed vocabulary in
# test/run.sh. An unknown directive is an error and not a shrug.
# `command` is argv, split on whitespace, run through test/lib/step.sh. It does
# not name the artifact: `build=` and `app=` do that, and run.sh appends the
# paths it just built. It also does not name the toolkit or the screenshot
# directory -- see lanes.tsv, and the `shots=` directive.
# File order is run order, and with one list it is one order: each lane runs the
# subsequence of these rows that names it, and CI runs it exactly so -- every
# bash lane in ci.yml is provisioning, one `bash test/run.sh <lane>` step, and
# the sheet. That step was seventeen on gjs, one per row, each carrying a
# `timeout-minutes` that had to be kept equal to the row's leash by hand and an
# `if: always()` that had to be remembered, and each with the same essay above
# it as the same step on four other lanes. The essays are here now, once each,
# above the rows they are about.
# What the one step changes about a run: nothing is skipped any more. Under one
# step per suite, a red `walk` skipped `attack`, `early` and `netinstall` behind
# it, and only the standards probes, gated `if: always()`, still ran. run.sh
# runs every row and exits the failure count, so a red suite costs its own
# reading and no other -- which is the rule the gated steps were written to,
# applied to the whole lane. The bound on a suite is its row's `timeout=`,
# with the lane's default behind it, and the job's own ceiling is the backstop
# for a hang the leash did not catch.
# The order fits every lane as CI ran it but one: macos ran `walk` before
# `loaders` and the other four ran them the other way round, and no single
# sequence holds both. macos runs loaders first here.
# Provisioning is not a suite. apt, brew, sysctl, setup-zig, docker login, the
# engine-removal guards, anything reading a secret and anything with a ${{ }} in
# it stays in the workflow, which is the thing that owns the machine. So do the
# sheet and upload steps, and selftest.sh, which runs before the lane rather
# than in it because a broken reporter makes every reading behind it
# unreadable and is worth finding out first.
# A reading of the machine is a row, though, when a suite depends on it and the
# only thing it must not do is fail the lane: `shotroom` clears the macOS alert
# out of every picture the lane will take, exits 0 whatever it finds, and is
# `soft` so that its leash cannot fail it either. The line between the two is
# whether the step asks the machine something or tells it something.
# The Windows lanes' own suites have no rows: their steps are `shell: pwsh` and
# this column is argv for bash. Their builds do come from the tables --
# `run.sh --build <slot>=<build>` -- so what they run is declared even where how
# they run it is not. windows-launch's one bash step, netinstall, is a row.
# bsd and kde-live have no rows, and that is not a migration left half-done:
# bsd runs netinstall/test/run.sh inside a guest this runner cannot reach, and
# kde-live runs qtkde.sh, which is a container and not a suite.
# The launcher's own seatbelt profile, asserted as a value: that it can be
# built inside a profile that denies /tmp, that the text is the same either
# way, that seatbelt takes it, and that what seatbelt takes confines. Every
# other macOS suite launches the launcher and then asks about the window, and
# the window comes up with the profile silently missing -- which is how a
# here-document in a shell whose here-documents go to /tmp cost every
# netinstall launch its inner profile without one step going red. No display,
# no engine, about a second, so it sits at the top of the lane.
# Handed the artifact its row builds and parses, for parse.sh's own reason:
# this asserts what shipped, and the `@@include` that puts macos-confine.sh
# into a build is the step most able to go wrong. Naming it also keeps this
# suite off assemble.sh, which it would otherwise call for itself.
confine
# Asserted with stub interpreters: no display, no toolkit, and it is the only
# place the meaning of an exit status is checked rather than assumed -- which
# is the contract the fallthrough rests on. On macos it is about the platform
# whose order it asserts: lanes.sh ran on three Linux lanes and nowhere else,
# so the two assertions that name osascript had never executed, and the
# ordering that lane depends on was asserted only where osascript does not
# exist.
lanes
lanes
# The assembler, and the stamp it says it applied. Pure shell, no display and
# about a second, so it runs on every lane that assembles anything -- once per
# sed, because the spelling of what it asserts is sed's and the three seds
# here are not the same program. gjs is the GNU one, windows-launch is MSYS,
# macos is BSD. kde is ubuntu-latest as well and used to run it a fourth time
# against the very same GNU sed, which is the rule being read as "every lane"
# rather than as what it says; it is 9 s, the smallest thing to put back, and
# what leaving it out buys is that the rule means what it says. Every defect
# is measured against `oldbuild.sh`, the assembler as it shipped through PR
# 23, carried inside the suite.
# Bounded, because the first version of it was not: it launched the artifact
# and waited on it, the Windows lane went from twelve minutes to fifty and
# lost its runner, and a lane that dies publishes nothing -- so which step
# blocked was not readable afterwards. The suite no longer starts anything
# whose exit it does not control, and the leash is the second half of that.
# windows-launch runs it from its own step, because that lane's other suites
# are pwsh and interleave with it.
assemble
# The room, before anything is photographed in it. Every picture the macos
# lane published once carried the macOS re-authorisation alert -- "bash is
# requesting to bypass the system private window picker" -- centred on the
# display, over the app. It is raised by the first capture of the job and
# never times out, so one alert sat in all fourteen frames. Cropping to the
# window used to hide it, and hiding it is what the pictures stopped doing.
# An experiment and not a control: it names the process that presents the
# alert, tries the two things that might dismiss it, and prints what happened
# at each stage. It cannot fail the lane -- the script exits 0 whatever it
# finds, and the row is `soft`, so the leash cannot fail it either -- and its
# whole output is a reading for the next round. Before the first launch,
# because the point is to have the room settled before the first shutter, and
# because its own throwaway capture is then the one that provokes the alert
# rather than `00-initial`. macos-netinstall runs it for the splash's
# pictures, which carried the same alert until it did.
shotroom
# The Qt launch path's document, which no longer has a name. Every check is
# one that fails against the commit before it, and the payloads it plants are
# proven live against qml itself first.
# QTWEBENGINE_CHROMIUM_FLAGS and QML_XHR_ALLOW_FILE_READ live in
# test/suite/appdir.sh, which is the thing that drives qml directly and so is
# the thing that needs them. The first of the two carries a space, and this
# command column is argv split on whitespace -- that was the one thing that
# kept this suite a hand-written step.
appdir
# The loader environment the standalone launch path hands its engine. Every
# check here is against the same build with the fix cut out of it, so "it
# would have failed before" is measured in this run rather than claimed. Two
# builds go in: the testing tier, because the suite has to know the app came
# up and on two lanes that is scaffolding -- the macOS driver writes its title
# to a file only there, and Qt's Chromium needs the no-sandbox flag this
# container cannot do without -- and the default tier, which is the only build
# the sandbox section can ask its question of, since the testing tier is what
# puts --no-sandbox on the command line. Neither tier touches the environment.
# macos takes the testing build alone.
loaders
loaders
loaders
# Six states of one window, watched from outside. The root colour that a step
# used to set is test/suite/verify-linux.sh's now -- it is cosmetic, it exists
# for the pictures that file takes, and two of the four jobs that ran this
# were missing it. The renderer-sandbox check that sat beside the
# linux-engines step in four lines of shell is a case in that file too: it
# wrote FAIL to a step's stderr and reached no sheet, so a lane whose renderer
# stopped being sandboxed and a lane that never asked looked the same in the
# grid. gjs runs the same WebKitGTK and asks it too.
# kde is the one lane that launches the artifact under a session bus --
# QtWebEngine wants one and the container has no desktop to inherit it from
# -- which is what its row's `dbus` says.
# On macos this was once the last step in the lane with no way to be read,
# and it cost a merge: verify-macos.sh exits before its first screenshot when
# the window does not appear, so the artifact upload found nothing either,
# and the app's own account went to a log that was catted into the job log
# and carried no further. The app's output is appended to the verifier's log
# now, so one file carries both sides of the launch.
walk
walk
walk
# The app under test here is hostile page content. Built at the default tier
# on purpose: the lane is what says the shipped configuration refuses these,
# not a configuration assembled for the test. kde asks for `gtk` on top of its
# Qt defaults because the probe reaches its window through the GTK walk on
# that machine; macos builds the testing tier because there is no window a
# shell can query there, so the report reaches the verifier through the
# status file only a testing build writes.
attack
attack
attack
# A page that navigates before its own load has finished. Built at the
# default tier for the same reason the attack app is: the lane is what says
# the shipped configuration holds, not a configuration assembled for the
# test. The stall socket and the navigation target that have to be up before
# the app launches are test/suite/early.sh's, which is where the order they
# have to come up in is written down. kde's `gtk` is the attack row's, for the
# attack row's reason.
# On macos it is asserted like everywhere else since PR 6 gave that driver a
# guard to assert against -- -stopLoading from didStartProvisionalNavigation:,
# because WKNavigationDelegate takes a block for the policy decision and JXA
# cannot call one. That is the only lane that builds the probe at the testing
# tier, and it is not a preference: the report reaches the verifier through
# the status file only a testing build writes. test/builds.tsv carries both
# tiers. `at=held` with no control is what this reading is, and it stayed
# green through four PRs of the guard announcing its own failure on every
# launch; navrefuse, below, is where that build is put against itself.
early
early
early
# One row per lane and not one row, because the five lanes ask it five
# different questions and each asks in its own variables. gjs runs the whole
# list under X11 and photographs the splash; wayland runs the splash alone --
# the rest of the list asks what a kernel refuses, and this lane is
# ubuntu-latest like gjs and kde -- under a compositor its lane row brings up
# beside the X server, because two of the splash's cases are about the choice
# between the two and can be asked nowhere else; kde runs the toolkit-facing
# suites alone -- this lane and gjs are both ubuntu-latest, one kernel, one
# Landlock ABI, so every suite that asks what the kernel refuses was being
# asked twice on the same machine, about 170 s a push; netinstall/test/run.sh
# writes the argument out in full where NEUTRINO_SUITES is read -- under a
# session bus, because confine-session closes one and the session it closes
# has to have been really there. windows-launch and macos-netinstall run the
# whole list with no display of ours at all and assert which mechanism the
# splash drew with.
# The pictures: splash.sh photographs the splash window over a stalled
# download, one portrait and then six frames in a row, which the sheet plays
# back as one figure that cycles, because the window moves and a still cannot
# show that. `shots=` is where they go, beside the verifiers' frames and not
# among them, so the sheet can head them apart; NEUTRINO_SPLASH_SHOTS follows
# it inside splash.sh. NEUTRINO_SPLASH_EXPECT is an assertion and not a
# report: the splash declines silently where it cannot draw, so a lane that
# lost its display server would pass splash.sh by skipping every case in it.
# Measured on run 33750772253, not hoped for.
# The command is `dbus-run-session -- bash ...` on kde and not the `dbus`
# directive, because that directive puts a bus around the artifact step.sh
# launches, and here there is no artifact: the runner under it launches its
# own. NEUTRINO_SUITES takes commas as well as spaces for this column's sake.
# On windows-launch the compiler is the step's `env:`, not the row's: it is
# what setup-zig put on the machine, and a row is not the place to say what a
# machine has.
netinstall
netinstall
netinstall
column4: env NEUTRINO_SUITES=env,e2e QTWEBENGINE_DISABLE_SANDBOX=1 dbus-run-session -- bash netinstall/test/run.sh

column1: netinstall
netinstall
# The navigation guard PR 6 built, and the account it gives of itself. It
# shipped spelled `webViewRef.stopLoading()`, and JXA runs a zero-argument
# selector when the property is read -- so the read stopped the load and the
# `()` after it threw, and for four PRs the guard refused every navigation and
# logged that it could not. Nothing else could catch that: verify-attack.sh
# aims at a host that never resolves, so its `nav` field is free whatever the
# guard does, and verify-early.sh asserts `at=held` with no control -- and
# `held` was the reading before the fix and after it, because the guard was
# working the whole time.
# So this asserts the effect and the account separately, against a control
# that is this artifact with the refusal deleted and against the spelling the
# fix replaced. Three launches of the same build, one line apart.
navrefuse
# The apparatus, and nothing else. Two questions were opened here. Whether an
# app can be written against `window.resizeTo` and `window.outerWidth` instead
# of against `neutrino.window.resize` and nothing at all; and whether an
# assignment to `document.title` reaches the native title. Both are answered
# now -- the standard spellings are written over the engine's, and the
# launcher connects each engine's title-changed signal to the window -- and
# neither was answered by this round. What this round is for is the
# instruments: verify-std.sh records a window's title and geometry in one loop
# with nothing slow in it, and until that loop is known to read a live window
# and to see it change, every pair of numbers it prints later is
# unattributable.
# So both apps mutate the window through the API that already works, and the
# verifier fails its own control when it cannot see the mutation. A run where
# the harness reads the same geometry either side of a resize has not measured
# the engine's `outerWidth`; it has measured a window that never moved, or an
# instrument pointed at the wrong one.
# After everything that asserts, which is one half of a rule the workflow
# used to spell as `if: always()`. A probe must not fail a lane -- these
# verifiers exit non-zero only when a control fails, never for a reading. And
# a lane must not fail a probe: a suite ahead of this going red for unrelated
# reasons once skipped the probe behind it and cost a whole round for a step
# that could not have made the lane worse. run.sh runs every row now, so the
# second half holds for the whole lane and no gate has to be remembered.
# The two probes are separate rows and separate apps. The geometry app is
# written never to close, so if the first fails to reap it its window is still
# up when the second begins -- which is why they search for `^STD-GEOM-` and
# `^STD-DOC-` and not for a shared prefix.
stdgeom
stddoc
# Whether the standard window verbs do anything and can be taken over if they
# do not, and whether `neutrino.theme` is redundant with CSS. Round 1 is what
# earns these their place: it said the recording loop keeps up on every lane,
# that the size arithmetic agrees with the one engine that reports its own
# outer size, and -- on macOS -- that the file this platform reads titles
# through was being written wrong. Stacking these on an unvalidated
# instrument would have made one red cost four readings instead of one.
# The window probe's own control is the phase order: the launcher's API is
# exercised *after* the four native calls, because "resizeTo did nothing" and
# "the window stopped responding" are the same reading otherwise. The theme
# probe's is a colour keyword no engine can resolve, so that "unsupported" is
# distinguishable from a value -- and this round deliberately does not flip
# the desktop palette, so it reports what each engine says and settles
# nothing about where the value came from.
stdwin
stdtheme
# A desktop built so the media query is wrong about it. The two rows above ask
# what the runner's desktop looks like, and both of its states -- Adwaita and
# Adwaita:dark -- are ones where WebKitGTK happens to be right. That is not
# the engine reading the palette. On WebKitGTK `prefers-color-scheme` follows
# the theme's *name*: the prefer-dark flag, or a name carrying the dark
# variant. Adwaita:dark carries it, so the flip cannot produce the
# disagreement this exists for and reported `agreed=YES` on every lane for two
# rounds.
# Mint ships some twenty themes that do produce it -- `Mint-Y-Dark-Grey` and
# the rest of the `-Dark-<colour>` families are the same dark grey as
# `Mint-Y-Dark`, named for the accent instead of the variant, and measured
# dark by this launcher and light by the engine. None of them is on the
# image, so themescheme.sh writes the theme it needs and asserts that it
# loaded before it asserts anything about the query.
# This is the suite that fails with the force taken out of the launcher,
# which is the only reason it exists.
themescheme
# Where each colour came from. The single-launch theme row above says what an
# engine reports and nothing about provenance, and that gap is not
# hypothetical. WebKit hardcodes Highlight one unit from Adwaita's accent, so
# on a default GNOME desktop it reads exactly like an engine following the
# palette -- round 2 recorded it as doing so, and it does not. Flipped to
# Adwaita:dark the desktop's accent moved and Highlight did not.
# So this launches twice with the desktop flipped between and asks one
# question of each value: did it move. themeflip.sh owns the sequencing
# because two parts of it are easy to get wrong and invisible in YAML -- the
# knob is cleared before it is set, each half, and the second half refuses to
# start while the first half's window is still up, since both answer to the
# same title prefix and a stale reading does not announce itself.
# The differential's middle control is what fails a lane whose knob does not
# work: better a red suite that says the flip did not take than a green one
# reporting fifteen constants it never disturbed. Late in the lane, so that
# costs its own reading and nothing else. macos carries the live half's app
# beside it.
themeflip
themeflip
column3: timeout=840 cat=flip-a cat=flip-b cat=flip-live-app build=std-theme build=live:live-theme

column1: # Which until this row existed was the one artifact in this tree nobody ran.
# Everything else here builds a probe written by someone who knew which lanes
# need a document waited for. pages/demo is written the way the README tells
# an author to write an app, and it is what people actually download -- so it
# is the artifact whose defects reach users first, and it shipped with a Close
# button that did nothing on Windows. What found that was a person on Windows
# Home, not this file.
# test/build/demoapp.sh builds the published four files with a reporter
# concatenated onto the end of the app's own script; the app itself is
# unmodified, because the point is to measure what ships.
demo
# Three rows, because they are three different kinds of thing.
# The probe asks the *toolkit* what roles it can name and which signals move
# when the desktop's font moves. What it measures is a report and not a case;
# whether it could take the reading at all is a case, and it is counted -- the
# workflow kept continue-on-error on this step after the row stopped being
# soft, and a probe that raised on its first line went green there once. On
# macos it is the only standing instrument of its kind: there is no live test
# there, because macOS publishes no notification for a UI font change and no
# scriptable knob to test one against, so it is what would notice a macOS
# release moving a family, a size, or what weightOfFont: answers. kde has no
# probe any more: fontprobe.qml's three questions are answered and none of
# them can change -- Qt exposes one role and no others, both size fields are
# present with no -1 hazard, and the no-NOTIFY refusal was measured verbatim
# on real Plasma 6 with KDEPlasmaPlatformTheme6 loaded.
# stdfont asserts. verify-std.sh's font mode fails a lane where
# `neutrino.fonts` and the custom properties disagree, where an unset property
# does not reach the generic beside it, or -- on WebKitGTK, which reads the
# same desktop independently through the CSS2 keywords -- where the two sizes
# differ by more than the pixel WebKit truncates.
# And fontlive is a running app with the desktop's fonts moved underneath it.
# stdfont launches once and reads once, so a watcher that never fires passes
# it. This is the twin of the live theme half and it closes the same gap: the
# palette lane has already paid once for an observer that registered, raised
# nothing, and never fired. Two flips, because the two roles move by different
# knobs -- `ui` through GtkSettings and `monospace` through GSettings alone.
fontflip
fontflip
stdfont
fontlive
# The Windows lanes' suites are PowerShell, and this column is argv for
# bash; what makes them rows anyway is that MSYS bash can start pwsh, step.sh
# can leash it, log it and reap after it, and run.sh hands it the artifact
# spelled the way cmd.exe reads it. A suite that names its artifact by a
# parameter ends its command with that parameter, because run.sh appends the
# path last; one that reads $args takes it positionally. `reap=` on a row
# with no `app=` reaps the first build's slot by process name after the
# suite, which is what the steps did by hand with Get-Process. A suite the
# runner launches with `app=` is not a row here yet: step.sh launches with
# bash, and on this platform the artifact is cmd.exe's.
psparse
